Emma Tucker
 
America’s Own Banks Are a Weak Link in the Campaign to Cut Off Iran
 
Plus, Ukraine considers legalizing porn to fund its war chest, and carmakers add gas engines to boost EV range
 
 
MORTEZA NIKOUBAZL/NURPHOTO VIA GETTY IMAGES
 

1. FROM MY DESK

 

Good morning. As the fighting between the U.S. and Iran escalates over the Strait of Hormuz, the Trump administration has also been tightening its economic squeeze on Tehran. Yet billions of dollars of Iranian funds are still flowing through American banks each year. In 2024 alone, the Treasury identified about $9 billion in Iranian funds that moved through U.S. lenders. Iran uses foreign partners, front companies and other means to disguise the transactions, making them difficult to detect. Rory Jones and Dylan Tokar explain how Iran exploits the U.S.-led financial system and why stopping it isn’t so simple.

 

Turning to domestic politics, the Democratic Socialists of America are using an endless buffet of social events to attract new members and more closely bind existing ones to the movement. From “Coffee With Comrades” and socialist softball to karaoke and speed dating, Joshua Chaffin and Maya Davis look at how fast-growing chapters are trying to turn the “DSA-curious” into active members.

 

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here. If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.

 
 
 

2. TODAY’S HEADLINES

 

• President Trump’s super PAC is pouring $10 million into the Texas Senate race to back Republican Ken Paxton as he faces Democrat James Talarico.

 

• Ukraine is considering legalizing pornography, with lawmakers arguing that taxing the industry could raise up to $25 million a year for the war effort.

 

• Two men without lawyers beat long odds to get their cases before the Supreme Court, breaking through a system dominated by elite attorneys.

 

• Hospitals and doctors’ offices are increasingly asking patients to pay upfront before getting medical procedures.

 
 
 

3. FROM THE MARKETS

 

• Everyday investors are handing their stock portfolios over to AI agents, turning themselves into mini quant funds. The technology can automate sophisticated trading strategies, but skeptics warn it could expose less-experienced investors to new dangers.

 
 
 

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

 

They left mainstream life to stake a claim to the West Bank in the name of God.

 

Known as Hilltop Youth, the loose network of young Israeli squatters live as nomads and aim to snuff out any chance of a future Palestinian state, often through violence and intimidation. They establish the barest of footholds on open land with temporary lodgings, sometimes planting an Israeli flag or a Star of David fashioned from scrap metal. Some later build homes and raise families; others simply keep away anyone but Jewish settlers. Feliz Solomon and Shoshanna Solomon report on how a movement that views its mission as transcending secular laws is testing the limits of Israel’s pro-settler government.

 

5.

 

Carmakers have a new idea to boost EV range: Add a gas engine.

 

The auto industry has a new solution to Americans’ fear that electric vehicles will run out of juice. Hyundai, Ford and Jeep parent Stellantis are planning a new kind of plug-in vehicle called an extended-range EV. It drives on electricity but comes with the security blanket of a gas-powered generator to recharge the battery when needed. One planned Ram pickup truck promises up to 690 miles of driving, more than twice the typical EV in the U.S. Christopher Otts shows how these extended-range EVs work and explains why carmakers are betting on this middle ground.

6. SEE THE STORY

 

Taiwan’s temples offer a glimpse of what China could have been.

 
 
Longshan Temple in Taipei. SEAN MARC LEE
 

In Taipei, temples are everywhere, wedged between shops and apartment blocks, their incense smoke wafting into busy intersections. On weekday mornings, they’re packed with ordinary people burning offerings and whispering prayers. It’s a striking sight for Chinese-born reporter Lingling Wei, who grew up in a country where religion is tightly managed by the state. Follow her along as she takes you inside Taiwan’s temples, where decades of separation from China have allowed faith and folk traditions to flourish.

 
 
 

7. HAPPENING THIS WEEK

 

• Tuesday: New Hampshire holds primary elections. The 81st United Nations General Assembly opens.

 

• Wednesday: Rhode Island holds primary elections. Apple holds its annual fall product event, where it is expected to unveil a foldable iPhone. The NFL season kicks off. The Republican midterm convention begins in Dallas.

 

• Thursday: The Labor Department releases the August producer-price index.

 

• Friday: The Labor Department releases the August consumer-price index. The U.S. marks the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks.

 
 
 

8. THE NUMBER

 
15%
 

That’s how much Jersey City raised its municipal property-tax rate in late August to help close a budget gap. The city was facing an estimated $255 million deficit, and some argued it was relying too heavily on emergency borrowing and one-time money such as pandemic-relief funds and land sales. The increase comes despite a real-estate boom that helped the city’s population grow. Residents are baffled that a growing city is having such a money problem, with some homeowners threatening to leave.

 
 
 

9. AND FINALLY…

 

Which sleep-tracker data can you actually trust?

 

Our Personal Tech columnist Nicole Nguyen put her Oura ring to the test after it logged a two-hour binge-watching session as sleep. At a Stanford sleep lab, she found that wearables can struggle to distinguish between different sleep stages because they can’t read brain waves. But some of their data is surprisingly reliable. Nicole breaks down which numbers you can trust, which to take with a grain of salt and when you might be better off ignoring your tracker altogether.
